tasks.title: Vertex, Linear Rewrite, and Crossings of a Line and a Parabola
tasks.context: Consider the following linear and quadratic functions: $f(x) = 4x + 2$ and $g(x) = x^{2} - x - 2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The point on the graph of $g(x)$ with the lowest $y$ coordinate is $\left(\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{9}{4}\right)$.
There exist values $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $g(x) = a f(x)^{2} + b f(x) + c$.
The sum of the roots of function $g(x)$ is $-1$.
The graph of the function $f(x) - g(x)$ intersects with the $y$-axis at $y = 0$.
The graphs of the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ intersect more than twice.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A parabola turns exactly once, at the axis of symmetry. The axis is read from the first two coefficients, and the lowest point (the leading coefficient is positive) is the value of $g$ there.

$$x=-\frac{-1}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=\frac{1}{2}$$

Substitute that abscissa into the given rule, term by term.

$$
g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}-2
$$

$$g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{9}{4}$$

The arms open upwards, so this vertex is the unique lowest point on the graph: every other input makes the square $(x-1/2)^{2}$ strictly positive and lifts the height.

The lowest point is $\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{9}{4}\right)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Write $f(x)=4x+2$ and try to match $g$ against a combination of $f^{2}$, $f$ and a constant. Squaring a non-constant line already produces an $x^{2}$ term, so the leading coefficient of $g$ can always be absorbed.

$$g(x)=A(4x+2)^{2}+B(4x+2)+C$$

Equating coefficients of $x^{2}$, then $x$, then the constant term, yields a unique triple.

$$A=\frac{1}{16}$$

$$B=-\frac{1}{2}$$

$$C=-\frac{5}{4}$$

Substituting these three numbers back reproduces $g$ identically: the $x^{2}$ term is $A\cdot 16=1$, and the remaining two powers then match as well.

A real triple therefore exists.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Vieta reads the sum of the roots straight off the coefficients: minus the middle coefficient over the leading one, with no quadratic formula required.

$$S=-\frac{b}{a}$$

$$S=-\frac{-1}{1}$$

$$S=1$$

The same sum is visible after factoring, which also names the two roots individually.

$$g(x)=(x+1)(x-2)$$

$$(-1)+2$$

$$g(x)=1$$

The claimed $-1$ is the product of dropping the minus sign in $-b/a$, or of reading the middle coefficient as if it were already the sum.

The sum of the roots is $1$, not $-1$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The graph of $f-g$ meets the $y$-axis at the single point where $x=0$, so the claimed height $y=0$ is a statement about the constant term of the difference.

$$(f-g)(x)=(4x+2)-(x^{2}-x-2)$$

$$(f-g)(x)=-x^{2}+5x+4$$

$$(f-g)(0)=4$$

The intercept is $y=4$, not $y=0$. Equivalently, $f(0)=2$ while $g(0)=-2$, so the two original graphs already sit four units apart on the vertical axis.

$$f(0)-g(0)=2-(-2)$$

$$f(0)-g(0)=4$$

The difference misses the origin on that axis.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A meeting of the two graphs is a root of $g-f$. Subtracting a line from a parabola leaves a parabola, and a quadratic equation has at most two real roots.

$$g(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-5x-4$$

The discriminant decides how many of those roots are real.

$$\Delta=(-5)^{2}-4(1)(-4)$$

$$\Delta=41>0$$

A positive discriminant gives exactly two distinct real meetings. A third meeting would require the difference to become cubic, which subtracting a line cannot do.

Two is the maximum a line and a parabola can manage.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem hands over a concrete line and a concrete parabola.

$$
f(x) = 4x+2\qquad g(x)
$$

$$
= x^{2}-x-2
$$

The axis of $g$ is read from the first two coefficients, and the vertex is the value of $g$ there. Meetings of the two graphs are the roots of the quadratic $f-g$, of which there can be at most two. Because $f$ is a non-constant line, the three maps $f^{2}$, $f$ and $1$ already span every parabola. Vieta still reads the sum of the roots of $g$ as $-b/a$, without solving.

tasks.title: Slope and Opening at a Glance
tasks.context: A line and a parabola are given by $f(x)=3x-5$ and $g(x)=-2x^{2}+x+4$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The slope of $y=f(x)$ is $3$.
The parabola $g$ opens upwards.
The slope of $y=f(x)$ is $-3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write the given line in the slope-intercept shape $y=mx+q$. The number in front of $x$ is the slope: it is the change of height for each unit step to the right.

$$f(x)=3x-5$$

$$m=3$$

The constant term $-5$ only shifts the graph vertically and does not tilt it.

Checking a unit step recovers the same coefficient, because the constant $-5$ cancels.

$$f(1)-f(0)=(3-5)-(-5)$$

$$f(1)-f(0)=3$$

That difference is the slope, independent of where the step is taken.

The slope is $3$, the number the claim names.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The opening of a parabola is the sign of the coefficient of $x^{2}$. Nothing else — not the linear term, not the constant term — can flip the arms.

$$g(x)=-2x^{2}+x+4$$

$$a=-2<0$$

A negative leading coefficient turns the arms downwards, so the vertex is a highest point rather than a lowest one.

A test on either side of the axis makes the downward opening visible: the graph is lower at $x=1$ than at the vertex.

$$x=-\frac{1}{2\cdot(-2)}$$

$$x=\frac{1}{4}\qquad g(1)$$

$$x=-2+1+4$$

$$x=3$$

The vertex height $g(1/4)$ is larger than $g(1)$, so the arms run downwards.

The parabola opens downwards, which is the opposite of the claim.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The value $f(0)$ is the height at which the line crosses the $y$-axis, obtained by killing every term that still contains $x$.

$$f(x)=3x-5$$

$$f(0)=3\cdot 0-5$$

$$f(0)=-5$$

Only the constant term survives, and that constant is already $-5$.

Geometrically this is the $y$-intercept of the line: the graph meets the vertical axis at $(0,-5)$.

$$f(0)=-5$$

No other term of $3x-5$ survives at $x=0$.

The computed value is $-5$, exactly the number claimed.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The same reading on the parabola: every term with an $x$ dies at the origin, so $g(0)$ is the constant term.

$$g(x)=-2x^{2}+x+4$$

$$g(0)=-2\cdot 0^{2}+0+4$$

$$g(0)=4$$

That height $4$ is where the parabola crosses the $y$-axis.

Geometrically this is the $y$-intercept of the parabola: the graph meets the vertical axis at $(0,4)$.

$$g(0)=4$$

The $x^{2}$ term and the $x$ term both die at the origin.

The computed value is $4$, the number named in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The slope is the coefficient of $x$, not the negative of that coefficient and not the constant term.

$$f(x)=3x-5$$

One extra unit of $x$ adds $3$ to the height, which is a rise, so the slope cannot be negative.

$$f(1)-f(0)=3$$

A negative slope would mean the graph falls as $x$ grows. Here a unit step raises the height.

$$f(2)-f(1)=1$$

The change is positive, so the slope cannot be $-3$.

The slope is $3$, not $-3$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
A line and a parabola are written with numbers already in place.

$$
f(x) = 3x-5\qquad g(x)
$$

$$
= -2x^{2}+x+4
$$

The slope of a line is the coefficient of $x$, and the constant term of either formula is the height on the $y$-axis. The opening of $g$ is decided by the sign in front of $x^{2}$ and by nothing else. A claimed slope with the wrong sign is the same coefficient with a minus attached, which a unit step $f(1)-f(0)$ immediately rejects.

tasks.title: Axis from Coefficients
tasks.context: The parabola $g$ and the line $f$ have the rules $g(x)=x^{2}-6x+5$ and $f(x)=2x+1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The axis of symmetry of $g$ is $x=3$.
$g$ opens downwards.
The slope of $f$ is $2$.
The axis of $g$ is $x=-3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A parabola is symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex. That line is determined by the leading and the middle coefficient alone.

$$x=-\frac{-6}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=3$$

The constant term $5$ never enters the formula, so it cannot move the axis.

The same abscissa is the midpoint of the two roots of $g$, which factor as $(x-1)(x-5)$.

$$\frac{1+5}{2}$$

$$x=3$$

Both readings name the vertical line $x=3$.

The axis is the line $x=3$, exactly the line named in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The opening is the sign of the coefficient of $x^{2}$. Here that coefficient is the leading $1$.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-6x+5$$

$$a=1>0$$

A positive leading coefficient turns the arms upwards, which also makes the vertex a lowest point.

A test on either side of the axis shows the arms rising: $g(0)=5$ and $g(6)=5$, both above the vertex.

$$g(3)=-4$$

The vertex is a lowest point, which is the geometry of an upward opening.

The parabola opens upwards, which is the opposite of the claim.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The slope of $y=mx+q$ is the coefficient standing in front of $x$.

$$f(x)=2x+1$$

$$m=2$$

Each extra unit of $x$ therefore raises the line by $2$, and the constant $1$ only lifts the graph without tilting it.

A unit step on the line recovers the same coefficient.

$$f(1)-f(0)=(3)-(1)$$

$$f(1)-f(0)=2$$

The constant $1$ cancels, leaving the slope $2$.

The slope is $2$, the number the claim names.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The claim is a single substitution into the given parabola: replace every $x$ by $3$ and simplify term by term.

$$g(3)=3^{2}-6\cdot 3+5$$

$$g(3)=9-18+5$$

$$g(3)=-4$$

The same height is the vertex value, because $x=3$ is the axis.

$$g(x)=(x-3)^{2}-4$$

Completing the square makes the same height visible without expanding $3^{2}$ by hand.

At $x=3$ the square vanishes and only $-4$ remains.

The height at $x=3$ is $-4$, the number named in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The axis formula uses the first two coefficients and produces a positive abscissa here, not a negative one.

$$x=-\frac{-6}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=3$$

The number $-3$ would be the result of dropping the minus sign in $-b/(2a)$.

$$-\frac{b}{2a}\neq\frac{b}{2a}$$

The number $-3$ would be $b/(2a)$, which is the axis formula with the outer minus dropped.

$$\frac{b}{2a}=\frac{-6}{2}$$

$$\frac{b}{2a}=-3$$

The correct formula keeps that minus, and produces $x=3$.

The axis is $x=3$, not $x=-3$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The two rules are concrete, so the axis formula and a single substitution settle the geometric claims.

$$
f(x) = 2x+1\qquad g(x)
$$

$$
= x^{2}-6x+5
$$

The axis of $g$ sits at $x=-b/(2a)$, independent of the constant term. Completing the square on the same parabola recovers the height on that axis. Dropping the minus sign in $-b/(2a)$ is the usual way to land on the opposite abscissa $x=-3$.

tasks.title: A Taxi Fare That Grows With the Distance
tasks.context: A taxi charges a fixed call-out fee plus a fixed amount per kilometre, so the fare in euros after $x$ kilometres is $C(x)=3x+5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: At $x=4$ the fare equals $17$ euros.
Each extra kilometre changes the fare by $3$ euros.
The fare changes by the same amount for every extra kilometre.
The fare equals $20$ euros at $x=5$.
Doubling $x$ always doubles the fare.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The fare after four kilometres is the value of the linear model at that distance, so insert $x=4$ and add the two terms.

$$C(x)=3x+5$$

$$C(4)=3\cdot 4+5$$

$$C(4)=12+5$$

$$C(4)=17$$

Reading the equation backwards checks the same pair: $3x+5=17$ forces $x=4$.

The same pair can be read backwards: the unique input that produces a fare of $17$ is $x=4$.

$$3x+5=17\qquad x$$

$$3x+5=4$$

No other distance yields that fare on this line.

The call-out of $5$ euros together with $3$ euros per kilometre produces $17$ euros.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

On a line, one extra unit of the input always changes the output by the same amount, and that amount is the slope.

$$C(x+1)-C(x)=\bigl(3(x+1)+5\bigr)-(3x+5)$$

$$C(x+1)-C(x)=3$$

The difference does not contain $x$ any more, so every extra kilometre costs the same $3$ euros.

Checking two concrete kilometres shows the same jump.

$$C(2)-C(1)=(11)-(8)$$

$$C(2)-C(1)=3$$

The jump does not depend on which kilometre is the extra one.

Each extra kilometre changes the fare by $3$ euros.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Equal steps of the input produce equal changes of the fare only when the model is a line; a square term would make the steps grow.

$$C(x)=3x+5$$

$$C(x+1)-C(x)=3$$

The first difference is the constant $3$, independent of how far the taxi has already gone.

A square term would make later kilometres cost more than earlier ones. This model has no $x^{2}$ term.

$$C(10)-C(9)=3$$

$$C(10)-C(9)=C(2)-C(1)$$

Equal input steps produce equal fare jumps, which is the definition of a line.

The change per kilometre is the constant slope.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The claim pins the fare to one figure, so read the model as an equation and see which input produces that figure.

$$3x+5=20$$

$$x=5$$

Substituting the claimed input back into the model checks the pair.

$$C(5)=3\cdot 5+5$$

$$C(5)=20$$

The arithmetic is the same substitution at a neighbouring input.

$$C(5)=15+5$$

$$C(5)=20$$

Five kilometres at $3$ euros each, plus the $5$ euro call-out, is $20$ euros.

The fare at that input really is $20$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Doubling the input doubles the output only for a model whose graph runs through the origin. A constant call-out is charged once and is not doubled with the rest.

$$C(1)=8\qquad C(2)$$

$$C(1)=11$$

Twice the value at $x=1$ would be $16$, whereas the model gives $11$ at $x=2$.

$$C(2x)=6x+5\neq 2(3x+5)$$

A model through the origin would double when $x$ doubles. The leftover constant $5$ breaks that proportion at every scale.

$$C(2x)=6x+5\qquad 2C(x)$$

$$C(2x)=6x+10$$

The two right-hand sides differ by $5$ for every $x$.

The leftover constant $5$ breaks the proportion.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The fare is a single line: a fixed call-out plus a constant charge per kilometre.

$$C(x)=3x+5$$

The slope $3$ is the change of fare for each extra kilometre, and the constant $5$ is charged once. Doubling $x$ therefore cannot double $C$, because that constant is not doubled with the rest. Every claimed fare is a substitution into this one model, and the first difference $C(x+1)-C(x)$ is the constant $3$.

tasks.title: Intercept Checklist
tasks.context: Start from the line $f(x)=5x$ and the parabola $g(x)=x^{2}-4$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $g$ has roots $2$ and $-2$.
The slope of $f$ is $5$.
$g$ opens downwards.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The line $f(x)=5x$ runs through the origin, so its height at $x=0$ is the constant term, which is absent and therefore $0$.

$$f(0)=5\cdot 0$$

$$f(0)=0$$

Geometrically this is the $y$-intercept: the graph meets the vertical axis at the origin.

The same vanishing is the $y$-intercept of a line through the origin.

$$f(x)=5x\qquad f(0)$$

$$f(x)=0$$

There is no constant term that could lift the graph off $(0,0)$.

The computed value is $0$, the number claimed.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The roots are the abscissas at which the graph meets the $x$-axis. The given formula is a difference of squares, so it factors at sight.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4$$

$$g(x)=(x-2)(x+2)$$

$$x=2\qquad x$$

$$x=-2$$

Both factors vanish at the two numbers the claim names, and no other real root exists.

Substituting either claimed root back into $g$ confirms a zero.

$$g(2)=4-4$$

$$g(2)=0\qquad g(-2)$$

$$g(2)=4-4$$

$$g(2)=0$$

No other real $x$ kills a difference of squares $x^{2}-4$.

The roots are $2$ and $-2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The slope of $y=mx+q$ is the coefficient of $x$. Here the line is $5x$ with no constant term.

$$f(x)=5x$$

$$m=5$$

Each extra unit of $x$ raises the height by $5$.

A unit step on this line through the origin raises the height by exactly $5$.

$$f(1)-f(0)=5$$

The constant term is absent, so nothing else contributes to the slope.

The slope is $5$, the number the claim names.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The opening is the sign of the leading coefficient, and here that coefficient is $+1$.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4$$

$$a=1>0$$

A positive leading coefficient turns the arms upwards (the graph of $y=x^{2}$ shifted down by $4$).

The graph of $y=x^{2}-4$ is the graph of $y=x^{2}$ slid down by $4$, which still opens upwards.

$$g(0)=-4\qquad g(3)$$

$$g(0)=5$$

Values to the right of the axis sit above the vertex, the geometry of $a>0$.

The parabola opens upwards, which is the opposite of the claim.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The value $g(0)$ is the constant term of the parabola, because every term with an $x$ dies at the origin.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4$$

$$g(0)=0^{2}-4$$

$$g(0)=-4$$

That height $-4$ is where the graph crosses the $y$-axis.

That height $-4$ is where the parabola crosses the $y$-axis, four units below the origin.

$$g(0)=-4$$

The $x^{2}$ term dies at $x=0$, leaving only the constant.

The computed value is $-4$, the number named in the claim.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem fixes a line through the origin and a difference of squares.

$$
f(x) = 5x\qquad g(x)
$$

$$
= x^{2}-4
$$

The slope and the two values at $x=0$ are read off the coefficients. The roots of $g$ are the solutions of $g(x)=0$, and the sign of the leading coefficient decides the opening. Factoring $g=(x-2)(x+2)$ names both zeros at sight, without the quadratic formula.

tasks.title: Simple Vertex Read
tasks.context: A completed-square parabola and a matching line are supplied: $g(x)=(x-2)^{2}+3$ and $f(x)=x-2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The vertex of $g$ is $(2,3)$.
The axis of $g$ is $x=2$.
$f$ and $g$ share the root $x=2$.
$g$ opens upwards.
The slope of $f$ is $1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Completed-square form $a(x-h)^{2}+k$ displays the vertex as the pair $(h,k)$ sitting in the formula. Here the square is already written out.

$$g(x)=(x-2)^{2}+3$$

The square vanishes at $x=2$ and nowhere else, and the constant beside it is the height $3$.

$$g(2)=0+3$$

$$g(2)=3$$

Expanding is unnecessary, but it recovers the same vertex from the axis formula.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4x+7\qquad x$$

$$g(x)=\frac{4}{2}$$

$$g(x)=2$$

Then $g(2)=3$, which is the same pair $(2,3)$.

The vertex is $(2,3)$, the point the claim names.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The axis of a completed-square parabola is the vertical line through the number that is being subtracted from $x$ inside the square.

$$g(x)=(x-2)^{2}+3$$

$$x=2$$

Equivalently, expand to $x^{2}-4x+7$ and run the axis formula:

$$-b/(2a)=4/2$$

$$-b/(2a)=2$$

.

Symmetry about $x=2$ is the identity $g(2+t)=g(2-t)$, which the completed square makes obvious.

$$g(2+t)=t^{2}+3$$

$$g(2+t)=g(2-t)$$

The axis is that unique vertical line of symmetry.

The axis is the line $x=2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A shared root is a number at which both formulas vanish, so test the proposed $x=2$ in each rule separately.

$$f(2)=2-2$$

$$f(2)=0$$

$$g(2)=(2-2)^{2}+3$$

$$g(2)=3$$

The line vanishes at $x=2$, but the parabola takes the vertex height $3$ there.

A root of $g$ would require the height $3$ to be zero, which it is not. The vertex sits three units above the $x$-axis.

$$g(2)=3\neq 0$$

The line and the parabola therefore cannot share the root $x=2$.

The proposed root is not shared.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The opening is the sign of the coefficient in front of the square. Expanding is unnecessary: $(x-2)^{2}$ already carries leading coefficient $+1$.

$$g(x)=(x-2)^{2}+3$$

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4x+7$$

$$a=1>0$$

Values on either side of the vertex sit above it, which is the geometry of an upward opening.

$$g(1)=4\qquad g(2)$$

$$g(1)=3\qquad g(3)$$

$$g(1)=4$$

The arms rise away from $(2,3)$.

A positive leading coefficient turns the arms upwards.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The slope of $f(x)=x-2$ is the coefficient of $x$, which here is the invisible $1$.

$$f(x)=1\cdot x-2$$

$$m=1$$

Each extra unit of $x$ raises the line by $1$; the constant $-2$ only shifts it down.

A unit step on $f$ raises the height by $1$, confirming the invisible coefficient.

$$f(3)-f(2)=1$$

The constant $-2$ cancels, leaving the slope $1$.

The slope is $1$, the number the claim names.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The parabola is already in completed-square form, which displays the vertex directly.

$$
g(x) = (x-2)^{2}+3\qquad f(x)
$$

$$
= x-2
$$

The axis is the vertical line through that vertex. A shared root would have to kill both formulas at the same input, so each formula has to be tested there separately. The opening is the sign in front of the square, and the slope of $f$ is the invisible $1$ in front of $x$.

tasks.title: Leading Coefficient Sign
tasks.context: Two functions are handed over already written out: $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}x+7$ and $g(x)=3x^{2}-x$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $g$ opens upwards.
The slope of $f$ is $7$.
The axis of $g$ is $x=\frac{1}{6}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The opening of $g$ is the sign of the coefficient of $x^{2}$. Factoring through $x$ does not change that leading $3$.

$$g(x)=3x^{2}-x$$

$$a=3>0$$

A positive leading coefficient turns the arms upwards, so the vertex is a lowest point.

Factoring as $x(3x-1)$ does not touch the leading $3$. Completing the square would keep the same $a=3>0$.

$$g(x)=3\left(x-\frac{1}{6}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{12}$$

The square is scaled by a positive number, so the arms open upwards.

The parabola opens upwards.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The value $g(0)$ is the constant term. The given formula $3x^{2}-x$ has no constant term at all.

$$g(0)=3\cdot 0^{2}-0$$

$$g(0)=0$$

Equivalently, $g$ factors as $x(3x-1)$, which is visibly $0$ at the origin.

The factor $x$ in $g(x)=x(3x-1)$ is the algebraic form of a root at the origin, which is also a $y$-intercept of $0$.

$$g(0)=0$$

There is no constant term that could lift the graph off $(0,0)$.

The graph crosses the $y$-axis at height $0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The slope is the coefficient of $x$, not the constant term. The constant $7$ is the $y$-intercept, which does not tilt the line.

$$f(x)=\frac{1}{2}x+7$$

$$m=\frac{1}{2}$$

Each extra unit of $x$ raises the height by only $\frac{1}{2}$, not by $7$.

A unit step on the line raises the height by only one half, not by $7$.

$$f(1)-f(0)=\frac{1}{2}$$

The number $7$ is the $y$-intercept $f(0)$, which does not tilt the graph.

The slope is $\frac{1}{2}$, not $7$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The height $f(0)$ is the constant term of the line, obtained by killing the term that still contains $x$.

$$f(x)=\frac{1}{2}x+7$$

$$f(0)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0+7$$

$$f(0)=7$$

That height $7$ is where the graph crosses the $y$-axis.

Geometrically this is the $y$-intercept: the graph meets the vertical axis at $(0,7)$.

$$f(0)=7$$

The slope term $\frac{1}{2}x$ dies at $x=0$.

The computed value is $7$, the number named in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The axis of $g$ is read from the first two coefficients, independent of any missing constant term.

tasks.title: Nested Functions Without Numbers
tasks.context: A non-constant line $f$ and a parabola $g$ are given, with no further numeric data. Judge the claims about nested functions. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Equal highest powers do not make the two composites the same function. The coefficients and the lower-degree terms generally differ.

Take $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}$.

$$g(f(x))=(x+1)^{2}$$

$$g(f(x))=x^{2}+2x+1$$

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

At $x=1$ one composite equals $4$ and the other equals $2$.

Take $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}$. At $x=1$ one composite equals $4$ and the other equals $2$.

$$g(f(x))=(x+1)^{2}\qquad f(g(x))$$

$$g(f(x))=x^{2}+1$$

The two nested functions are not identical.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Replacing $f$ by $f^{2}$ means the inner map now has highest power $2$. Nesting the parabola around that square multiplies the highest powers $2$ and $2$.

$$g\bigl(f(x)^{2}\bigr)=a\bigl(f(x)^{2}\bigr)^{2}+\cdots$$

$$g\bigl(f(x)^{2}\bigr)=a f(x)^{4}+\cdots$$

A non-constant line has $f(x)^{4}$ of highest power $4$, and the leading coefficient $a m^{4}$ is non-zero.

$$g\bigl(f(x)^{2}\bigr)=a f(x)^{4}+\cdots$$

The nested function has highest power $x^{4}$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Nesting two polynomials multiplies their highest powers instead of adding them.

$$
f(x) = mx+q\qquad g(x)
$$

$$
= ax^{2}+bx+c
$$

A line inside a parabola, or a parabola inside a line, therefore still produces highest power $2$. The two orders $g(f(x))$ and $f(g(x))$ are different functions in general. Replacing the inner map by $f^{2}$ multiplies an extra $2$ and reaches $x^{4}$.

tasks.title: Monotonicity: Line Versus Parabola
tasks.context: A general line $f(x)=mx+k$ with $m\neq 0$ is paired with a general parabola $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ with $a\neq 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $f$ is strictly monotone on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
$g$ is strictly monotone on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
On the half-line to the right of the axis of $g$, the restriction of $g$ is strictly monotone.
If $m>0$ and $a>0$, then $f(x)<g(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.
A constant function (slope zero) is still strictly monotone.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A non-constant line has a constant non-zero slope, so it never turns. If $m>0$ the graph rises on the whole real line; if $m<0$ it falls on the whole real line.

$$f(x_{2})-f(x_{1})=m(x_{2}-x_{1})$$

Whenever $x_{2}>x_{1}$, the difference has the sign of $m$ and cannot vanish. That is the definition of strict monotonicity on $\mathbb{R}$.

A non-constant line never turns.

$f$ is strictly monotone on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A parabola always turns at its axis. On one side of the axis it falls, and on the other side it rises (or the reverse, if $a<0$).

$$g'(x)=2ax+b\qquad g'\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right)$$

$$g'(x)=0$$

Take $g(x)=x^{2}$. Then

$$g(-1)=1$$

$$g(-1)=g(1)$$

 with $-1<1$, so $g$ is not strictly monotone on $\mathbb{R}$.

$$g'\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right)=0$$

A parabola always turns at its axis.

A parabola is not strictly monotone on the whole real line.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

On the half-line to the right of the axis, the derivative $g'(x)=2ax+b$ does not change sign: it keeps the sign of $a$.

$$x>-\frac{b}{2a}\implies 2ax+b\text{ has the sign of }a$$

If $a>0$ the restriction is strictly increasing; if $a<0$ it is strictly decreasing. In either case it is strictly monotone.

$$x>-\frac{b}{2a}\implies g'\text{ has the sign of }a$$

The restriction of $g$ to the right of the axis does not turn.

The restriction of $g$ to the right of the axis is strictly monotone.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

If $a>0$, then $g(x)$ grows like $ax^{2}$, which outruns any line $mx+k$ as $x\to +\infty$. The difference $g-f$ is a quadratic opening upwards, so it is eventually positive.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-k)$$

The leading coefficient $a>0$ forces $g(x)-f(x)\to +\infty$ as $x\to +\infty$, hence $f(x)<g(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+\cdots$$

The parabola overtakes the line.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A constant function has slope zero, so $f(x_{2})-f(x_{1})=0$ for every pair of inputs. Strict monotonicity requires that this difference never vanish when $x_{2}\neq x_{1}$.

$$f(x)=k\qquad f(1)-f(0)$$

$$f(x)=0$$

The graph is a horizontal line, which is monotone in the weak sense but not strictly monotone.

$$f(1)-f(0)=0$$

A constant function is not strictly monotone.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
A non-constant line keeps a constant slope, so it never turns.

$$
f(x) = mx+k\qquad g(x)
$$

$$
= ax^{2}+bx+c
$$

A parabola always turns at its axis, so it cannot be strictly monotone on the whole real line. On either half-line determined by that axis, the restriction of $g$ does not turn any more. A constant function has slope zero and is not strictly monotone.

tasks.title: Parameter Tangency Criterion
tasks.context: A general parabola $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ with $a\neq 0$ is compared with the family of lines $f_t(x)=tx+1$ parametrised by $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every real $t$, the line $y=f_t(x)$ is tangent to the graph of $g$.
There exists at least one real $t$ for which $y=f_t$ is tangent to $y=g$.
If $y=f_t$ is tangent to $y=g$ at $x_0$, then $g'(x_0)=t$.
If $g-f_t$ has two distinct real roots, then the graphs intersect at two points and are not tangent.
Replacing the intercept $1$ in $f_t$ by an arbitrary constant $q$ can change whether a tangent slope exists.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Tangency for a given slope $t$ is the vanishing of $\Delta(t)=(b-t)^{2}-4a(c-1)$. That quantity is a quadratic in $t$ and is not identically zero.

$$\Delta(t)=(t-b)^{2}-4a(c-1)$$

Take $g(x)=x^{2}$ and $t=0$: then $g-f_{0}=x^{2}-1$, whose discriminant is $4>0$, so $y=1$ cuts $y=x^{2}$ twice and is not tangent.

$$\Delta(0)=4\neq 0$$

Not every slope is tangent.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Setting $\Delta(t)=0$ produces $(t-b)^{2}=4a(c-1)$. A square can equal the right-hand side only when that side is non-negative.

$$(t-b)^{2}=4a(c-1)$$

If $a>0$ and $c<1$, the right-hand side is negative, so no real $t$ exists. Take $g(x)=x^{2}$: then $c=0<1$ and $4a(c-1)=-4<0$.

No real square equals $-4$, so this parabola admits no tangent of the form $tx+1$.

$$(t-b)^{2}=-4\text{ has no real }t$$

A tangent slope need not exist.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

If the graphs are tangent at $x_{0}$, they share a tangent line there, so their derivatives agree at that abscissa. The derivative of $f_{t}$ is the constant $t$.

$$g'(x_{0})=2ax_{0}+b$$

$$g'(x_{0})=t$$

Equivalently, $g-f_{t}$ has a double root at $x_{0}$, which forces $(g-f_{t})'(x_{0})=0$, hence $g'(x_{0})=t$.

Shared tangent lines have equal slopes.

Tangency at $x_{0}$ forces $g'(x_{0})=t$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Two distinct real roots of $g-f_{t}$ are two distinct meeting abscissas. Tangency requires a repeated root, which is incompatible with two distinct roots.

$$\Delta(t)>0\iff\text{two distinct meetings, not tangent}$$

A quadratic cannot have both a double root and two distinct roots at once.

Two distinct real roots of $g-f_{t}$ mean two crossings and no tangency.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Replacing the intercept $1$ by an arbitrary $q$ changes the constant term of $g-f$ from $c-1$ to $c-q$, which changes the discriminant condition.

$$(t-b)^{2}=4a(c-q)$$

For $g(x)=x^{2}$ the choice $q=1$ gives a negative right-hand side and no real $t$, while $q=-1$ gives

$$t^{2}=4$$

, hence $t=\pm 2$. Changing $q$ created two tangent slopes that were not there before.

For $g(x)=x^{2}$ the choice $q=1$ gives a negative right-hand side and no real $t$, while $q=-1$ gives

$$t^{2}=4$$

, hence $t=\pm 2$.

The intercept can change whether a tangent slope exists.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Tangency of $y=tx+1$ with a general parabola is a discriminant condition in $t$.

$$\Delta(t)=(b-t)^{2}-4a(c-1)$$

That square equals $4a(c-1)$ only when the right-hand side is non-negative, which a general triple $(a,b,c)$ need not grant. Changing the intercept of the line changes the constant term of $g-f_{t}$ and can therefore change the picture. Two distinct roots of $g-f_{t}$ are two crossings, not a touch.

tasks.title: Shifts and Scalings of a Parabola
tasks.context: Start from $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ with $a\neq 0$. Consider $g_1(x)=g(x-r)$, $g_2(x)=g(x)+s$, and $g_3(x)=\lambda g(x)$ with $\lambda\neq 0$. No numeric data. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The axis of $g_1$ is the axis of $g$ shifted by $r$ units to the right.
The axis of $g_2$ differs from the axis of $g$.
If $\lambda<0$, then $g_3$ opens in the opposite direction from $g$.
There exist $r\neq 0$ such that $g_1$ has a different axis from $g$ but the same leading coefficient.
$g_3$ always has the same roots as $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Replacing $x$ by $x-r$ slides the graph of $g$ to the right by $r$ units. The axis, being a vertical line attached to the graph, slides with it.

$$g_{1}(x)=a(x-r)^{2}+b(x-r)+c$$

The axis of $g_{1}$ is $x=h+r$, where $h=-b/(2a)$ was the axis of $g$.

$$x=h+r$$

A horizontal shift slides the axis with the graph.

The axis of $g_{1}$ is the axis of $g$ shifted by $r$ units to the right.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Adding a constant $s$ moves the graph vertically. A vertical move cannot change a vertical axis.

$$g_{2}(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c+s$$

The first two coefficients $a$ and $b$ are unchanged, so the axis formula $x=-b/(2a)$ is unchanged.

Take $g(x)=x^{2}$ and $s=1$: both $x^{2}$ and $x^{2}+1$ have axis $x=0$.

The first two coefficients $a$ and $b$ are unchanged, so the axis does not move.

The axis of $g_{2}$ is the same as the axis of $g$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The opening of $g_{3}=\lambda g$ is the sign of $\lambda a$. If $\lambda<0$, that product has the opposite sign from $a$.

$$g_{3}(x)=\lambda a x^{2}+\lambda b x+\lambda c$$

A change of sign of the leading coefficient flips the arms. Scaling $x^{2}$ by $-1$ produces $-x^{2}$, which opens downwards.

$$g_{3}(x)=\lambda a x^{2}+\cdots$$

If $\lambda<0$, then $g_{3}$ opens opposite to $g$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A horizontal shift changes $h$ but does not touch the leading coefficient $a$. Any $r\neq 0$ therefore moves the axis while leaving $a$ alone.

$$g_{1}(x)=a(x-h-r)^{2}+k$$

Take $g(x)=x^{2}$ and $r=1$. Then $g_{1}(x)=(x-1)^{2}$ has axis $x=1\neq 0$ and the same leading coefficient $1$.

Such a shift exists.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A root of $g_{3}$ is a number $x$ with $\lambda g(x)=0$. Because $\lambda\neq 0$, this is the same condition as $g(x)=0$.

$$\lambda g(x) = 0\iff g(x)$$

$$= 0$$

Scaling cannot add or remove zeros. The two functions vanish at exactly the same abscissas.

$g_{3}$ always has the same roots as $g$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Three elementary moves are applied to a general parabola.

$$
g_{1}(x) = g(x-r)\qquad g_{2}(x)
$$

$$
= g(x)+s\qquad g_{3}(x)
$$

$$
= \lambda g(x)
$$

A horizontal shift moves the axis; a vertical shift does not. Scaling by $\lambda\neq 0$ keeps the roots (it does not add or remove zeros) but flips the opening when $\lambda$ is negative. The leading coefficient of $g_{1}$ is still $a$, even though the axis has moved.

tasks.title: Double Composition and Leading Match
tasks.context: A line and a parabola are given by $f(x)=4x+2$ and $g(x)=x^{2}-x-2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ forces $A=\frac{1}{16}$, $B=-\frac{1}{2}$, $C=-\frac{5}{4}$.
Because $f-g$ can be mistaken for a cubic, the graphs may meet three times.
At the axis of $g$, the gap $f-g$ equals $\frac{17}{4}$.
Completing the square gives $g(x)=\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{9}{4}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ is a three-coefficient linear system. The $x^{2}$ coefficients force $A$ first, because only $Af^{2}$ produces $x^{2}$.

$$1=A\cdot 16\qquad A$$

$$1=\frac{1}{16}$$

Equating the $x$ coefficients then gives $B$, and the constant terms give $C$.

$$B=-\frac{1}{2}$$

$$C=-\frac{5}{4}$$

Substituting the three numbers back reproduces $g$ identically.

Substituting the three numbers back reproduces $g$ identically: $A\cdot 16=1$ recovers the leading coefficient.

$$A=\frac{1}{16}$$

Matching forces the claimed triple.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The difference $f-g$ is quadratic, not cubic: $f$ has no $x^{2}$ term that could combine with $g$ to raise the degree.

$$f(x)-g(x)=-x^{2}+5x+4$$

A quadratic equation has at most two real roots, so three meetings are impossible. The discriminant $25+16=41>0$ gives exactly two meetings. A quadratic cannot hide a third root.

$$f-g=-x^{2}+5x+4$$

The graphs meet twice, not three times.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The two orders of nesting are different maps. Evaluate both at the origin.

$$f(0)=2\qquad g(2)$$

$$f(0)=4-2-2$$

$$f(0)=0$$

$$g(0)=-2\qquad f(-2)$$

$$g(0)=-8+2$$

$$g(0)=-6$$

$$0\neq -6$$

Evaluate both nested orders at the origin and compare.

$$g(f(0))=0\qquad f(g(0))$$

$$g(f(0))=-6$$

Composition does not commute for this pair.

The two orders of nesting are different maps; a single input $x=0$ already separates them.

$$0\neq -6$$

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The vertical gap at the axis is the difference of the two heights there. First locate the axis, then evaluate both models.

$$x=\frac{1}{2}$$

$$
f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=4\qquad g\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)
$$

$$f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{9}{4}$$

The gap is $4-(-9/4)=25/4$, not $17/4$.

$$\frac{25}{4}\neq\frac{17}{4}$$

The gap is $4-(-9/4)=25/4$, not $17/4$. The number $17/4$ would be $f(1/2)-1$, dropping the vertex depth.

The gap at the axis is $\frac{25}{4}$, not $\frac{17}{4}$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Completing the square uses the axis $x=1/2$ as the shift. Half of the middle coefficient $-1$ is $-1/2$.

$$x^{2}-x-2=\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}-2$$

$$g(x)=\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{9}{4}$$

Expanding recovers $x^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{9}{4}=x^{2}-x-2$.

$$h=\frac{1}{2}$$

The shift is the axis, and the constant is the vertex height.

Completing the square gives the claimed formula.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The same concrete pair as a rewrite-and-vertex exercise.

$$
f(x) = 4x+2\qquad g(x)
$$

$$
= x^{2}-x-2
$$

Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ is a three-coefficient linear system. Completing the square displays the vertex, and the two nested evaluations $g(f(0))$ and $f(g(0))$ are different numbers in general. The difference $f-g$ stays quadratic, so three meetings cannot occur.

tasks.title: Parameter Window for Two Meetings
tasks.context: A fixed parabola $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+1$ is compared with the family of lines $f_k(x)=kx+1$ as the real parameter $k$ varies. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $k$, the graphs intersect at the point $(0,1)$.
There is a unique slope that makes the line touch the parabola at exactly one point.
That unique touch happens at the shared $y$-intercept $(0,1)$ and matches the slope of the parabola there.
Besides the shared $y$-intercept, the graphs can meet again at a point with positive $x$-coordinate.
There exists a real $k$ for which the graphs fail to meet.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Every line $f_{k}(x)=kx+1$ is built to pass through $(0,1)$, and the given parabola does too: its constant term is $1$.

$$g(0)=1\qquad f_{k}(0)$$

$$g(0)=1$$

The two graphs therefore share that $y$-intercept for every slope $k$. Algebraically, the difference always has a factor $x$.

$$g(x)-f_{k}(x)=x^{2}-(4+k)x$$

$$g(x)-f_{k}(x)=x\bigl(x-(4+k)\bigr)$$

The factor $x$ is the root at the origin, independent of $k$. The shared point is $(0,1)$.

The graphs intersect at $(0,1)$ for every $k$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A unique meeting means the remaining root of $g-f_{k}$ collides with $x=0$. After factoring out $x$, that remaining root is $x=4+k$.

$$g(x)-f_{k}(x)=x\bigl(x-(4+k)\bigr)$$

Collision with the origin is the linear equation $4+k=0$.

$$k=-4$$

For every other slope the second root is distinct from $0$, so there are two meetings. Thus exactly one slope produces a unique intersection point (a tangency).

A unique tangent slope exists.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The unique slope that collapses the two meetings is $k=-4$, obtained by forcing the second root $4+k$ to be $0$. At that slope the only meeting is the shared $y$-intercept $(0,1)$.

$$g(x)-f_{-4}(x)=x^{2}$$

$$g(x)-f_{-4}(x)=x\cdot x$$

The slope of the parabola at that same point is the derivative $g'(0)$.

$$g'(x)=2x-4$$

$$g'(0)=-4$$

The line through $(0,1)$ of slope $g'(0)$ is precisely $y=-4x+1$, which is $f_{-4}$. Matching derivatives at a shared point is the geometric form of tangency.

The unique touch happens at $(0,1)$ and matches $g'(0)$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Besides the shared root $x=0$, the second meeting of $g$ with $f_{k}$ sits at $x=4+k$. That abscissa is positive as soon as $k$ is larger than $-4$.

$$x=4+k>0\iff k>-4$$

Take the horizontal line of the family, $k=0$. The second meeting is then at $x=4$.

$$g(4)=16-16+1$$

$$g(4)=1\qquad f_{0}(4)$$

$$g(4)=1$$

The point $(4,1)$ has positive first coordinate, and it lies on both graphs.

A second meeting with positive $x$-coordinate exists.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Every line of the family already meets the parabola at $(0,1)$, independently of $k$. There is therefore no real $k$ for which the graphs fail to meet.

$$g(0)=f_{k}(0)$$

$$g(0)=1$$

The discriminant of $g-f_{k}$ is a square, hence never negative.

$$\Delta(k)=(4+k)^{2}\ge 0$$

It equals zero only at the tangent slope $k=-4$, which is still a meeting (a touch at the origin). For every other $k$ there are two meetings.

The graphs always meet.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Every line of the family shares the $y$-intercept of the given parabola.

$$
g(x) = x^{2}-4x+1\qquad f_{k}(x)
$$

$$
= kx+1
$$

The difference $g-f_{k}$ therefore always has a factor $x$, so $x=0$ is a meeting for every slope. Tangency is that remaining root colliding with the origin, which happens for exactly one $k$, namely the derivative $g'(0)$. For every other slope a second meeting exists, and it can be placed in $x>0$ by taking $k>-4$.

tasks.title: Scaled Roots and Nested Order
tasks.context: You are given $f(x)=5x-2$. The quadratic $g$ has roots $2$ and $4$ but leading coefficient $2$. Recover $g$, then evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ forces $A=\frac{2}{25}$.
The distance between the roots of $g$ is $2$.
Completing the square gives $g(x)=2(x-3)^{2}-2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A quadratic with roots $2$ and $4$ and leading coefficient $2$ is twice the product of the corresponding linear factors.

$$g(x)=2(x-2)(x-4)$$

$$g(x)=2(x^{2}-6x+8)$$

$$g(x)=2x^{2}-12x+16$$

Both claimed roots kill a factor, and the leading coefficient is the announced $2$.

$$g(2)=0\qquad g(4)$$

$$g(2)=0$$

The rebuilt formula is $2x^{2}-12x+16$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ begins by equating $x^{2}$ coefficients. The line has slope $5$, so $A\cdot 25$ must equal the leading $2$.

$$2=A\cdot 25\qquad A$$

$$2=\frac{2}{25}$$

The remaining coefficients $B$ and $C$ are then uniquely determined, but the claim only names $A$.

$$2=A\cdot 25$$

Matching forces $A=\frac{2}{25}$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The two orders of nesting are different maps. Evaluate both at the origin.

$$f(0)=-2\qquad g(-2)$$

$$f(0)=2\cdot 4+24+16$$

$$f(0)=48$$

$$g(0)=16\qquad f(16)$$

$$g(0)=80-2$$

$$g(0)=78$$

$$48\neq 78$$

Evaluate both nested orders at the origin and compare.

$$g(f(0))=48\qquad f(g(0))$$

$$g(f(0))=78$$

Composition does not commute for this pair.

The two orders of nesting are different maps; a single input $x=0$ already separates them.

$$48\neq 78$$

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The distance between two roots is the absolute difference of those two numbers, independent of the leading coefficient.

$$|4-2|$$

$$=2$$

The leading $2$ stretches the graph vertically and does not move the zeros. Vieta’s sum $6$ and product $8$ recover the same two roots.

The distance between the roots is $2$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The axis is the midpoint of the roots, $x=3$. Completing the square uses that shift, with leading coefficient $2$.

$$2x^{2}-12x+16=2(x^{2}-6x)+16$$

$$2x^{2}-12x+16=2\bigl((x-3)^{2}-9\bigr)+16$$

$$g(x)=2(x-3)^{2}-2$$

Expanding recovers $2(x^{2}-6x+9)-2=2x^{2}-12x+16$.

$$h=3\qquad k$$

$$h=-2$$

The vertex sits at the midpoint of the roots, at height $-2$.

Completing the square gives the claimed formula.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The monic factor $(x-2)(x-4)$ is scaled by the announced leading coefficient $2$.

$$
g(x) = 2(x-2)(x-4)\qquad f(x)
$$

$$
= 5x-2
$$

The distance between the roots is $|4-2|$, independent of that leading $2$. Completing the square on the expanded formula displays the vertex at the midpoint $x=3$. Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ reads $A$ from the ratio of leading coefficients, and the two nested orders disagree at $x=0$.

tasks.title: Average Rate Versus Instantaneous Slope
tasks.context: The parabola $g(x)=x^{2}-6x+5$ is paired with the line $f(x)=4x-8$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The average rate of change of $g$ on $[0,2]$ equals the slope of $f$.
There exists $c\in(0,2)$ with $g'(c)$ equal to that average rate.
Completing the square gives $g(x)=(x-3)^{2}-4$.
By Vieta, the sum of roots is $-6$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The average rate of $g$ on $[0,2]$ is the slope of the chord joining the two endpoints, a difference quotient that need not equal the slope of the neighbouring line $f$.

$$\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}=\frac{(4-12+5)-5}{2}$$

$$\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}=-4$$

The slope of $f$ is $4$. Those two numbers are negatives of each other, not equal.

$$-4\neq 4$$

The average rate is $-4$, not the slope of $f$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

The mean-value theorem supplies a point of $(0,2)$ where $g'$ equals the average rate of $g$ on that interval. Compute that average first, as a difference quotient.

$$\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}=\frac{(4-12+5)-5}{2}$$

$$\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}=-4$$

For a parabola the point can be found by solving a linear equation.

$$g'(x)=2x-6$$

$$2c-6=-4\qquad c$$

$$2c-6=1$$

The number $1$ lies in $(0,2)$. Directly: $g'(1)=-4$, which is the average rate on $[0,2]$.

Such a $c$ exists.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Completing the square uses the axis $x=3$ as the shift. Half of the middle coefficient $-6$ is $-3$.

$$x^{2}-6x+5=(x-3)^{2}-9+5$$

$$g(x)=(x-3)^{2}-4$$

Expanding recovers $x^{2}-6x+9-4=x^{2}-6x+5$.

$$h=3\qquad k$$

$$h=-4$$

The vertex is $(3,-4)$, which is the completed-square pair.

Completing the square gives the claimed formula.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Vieta’s sum is minus the middle coefficient over the leading one, not the middle coefficient itself.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-6x+5$$

$$S=-\frac{-6}{1}$$

$$S=6$$

The claimed $-6$ is $b$, not $-b/a$. The roots $1$ and $5$ add to $6$.

$$1+5$$

$$S=6$$

The sum of the roots is $6$, not $-6$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The nested value $f(g(0))$ is a two-step evaluation.

$$g(0)=5$$

$$f(5)=4\cdot 5-8$$

$$f(5)=12$$

The two substitutions produce $12$.

The inner parabola at the origin is the constant term $5$, and the line at $5$ is $12$.

The two substitutions must be done in this order: parabola first, then the line.

$$g(0)=5\qquad f(5)$$

$$g(0)=12$$

The nested value is $12$.

tasks.solution_overview:
The average rate of $g$ on an interval is a difference quotient, not the slope of a neighbouring line.

$$

$$

$$
= 4x-8

The mean-value theorem still produces a point of $(0,2)$ where $g'$ equals that average. Vieta’s sum is $-b/a$, and a nested evaluation $f(g(0))$ is two substitutions. Completing the square uses the axis $x=3$ as the shift.

tasks.title: When Does Vertical Shift Kill Meetings?
tasks.context: The line $f(x)=2x$ is compared with the vertically shifted family $g_s(x)=x^{2}-x-2+s$, where $s$ is a real shift. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: With no vertical shift, the graphs meet at two points.
A large enough upward shift can make the graphs miss each other.
There exists $s$ making the graphs tangent.
Vertical shifts can create a third intersection with $f$.
The axis of $g_s$ depends on $s$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

With $s=0$ the difference $g_{0}-f$ is a quadratic whose discriminant can be computed at sight.

$$g_{0}(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-3x-2$$

$$\Delta=9+8$$

$$\Delta=17>0$$

A positive discriminant gives two distinct real meetings. The two roots of $x^{2}-3x-2=0$ are genuine intersections of $g_{0}$ with $f$.

$$\Delta=17>0$$

With no vertical shift the graphs meet at two points.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

An upward shift increases the constant term of $g_{s}-f$, which eventually makes the discriminant negative.

$$g_{s}(x)-2x=x^{2}-3x+(s-2)\qquad\Delta$$

$$g_{s}(x)-2x=9-4(s-2)$$

$$g_{s}(x)-2x=17-4s$$

If $s>17/4$, then $\Delta<0$ and the graphs miss each other. Take $s=5$: then

$$\Delta=17-20$$

$$\Delta=-3<0$$

.

Take $s=5$: then

$$\Delta=17-20$$

$$\Delta=-3<0$$

, so the graphs miss each other.

$$\Delta=17-4s<0\iff s>\frac{17}{4}$$

A large enough upward shift makes the graphs miss.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Tangency is the vanishing of $\Delta=17-4s$. That linear equation in $s$ has the unique root $s=17/4$.

$$s=\frac{17}{4}$$

For that shift, $g_{s}-f$ is a perfect square times a constant, so the graphs touch at exactly one point. The value $17/4$ is a legitimate real shift.

A tangent shift exists.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A vertical shift of $g$ only changes the constant term of $g-f$. The difference stays quadratic, so it still has at most two real roots.

$$g_{s}(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-3x+(s-2)$$

The leading coefficient $1$ never cancels. A third intersection would require a cubic difference, which a vertical shift cannot create.

$$g_{s}-f=x^{2}-3x+(s-2)$$

Vertical shifts cannot create a third meeting.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The axis formula $x=-b/(2a)$ uses only the first two coefficients. The shift $s$ is absorbed into the constant term and never enters the formula.

$$x=-\frac{-1}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{1}{2}$$

This axis is the same for every $s$. Completing the square makes the same fact visible: $s$ is absorbed into the height $k$, not into $h$.

$$x=\frac{1}{2}$$

The axis of $g_{s}$ does not depend on $s$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
A vertical shift of $g$ changes only the constant term of $g-f$.

$$
f(x) = 2x\qquad g_{s}(x)
$$

$$
= x^{2}-x-2+s
$$

The discriminant of $g_{s}-f$ is linear in $s$, so it can be positive, zero or negative. The axis formula ignores the constant term, so $s$ cannot move the axis, and the difference stays quadratic. A third meeting would require a cubic difference, which a vertical shift cannot create.

tasks.title: Slope, Constant Term, Axis
tasks.context: Start from the line $f(x)=7x+2$ and the parabola $g(x)=x^{2}+6x$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The slope of $y=f(x)$ is $7$.
The parabola $g$ opens downwards.
The axis of symmetry of $g$ is $x=-3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The given line is already written as $mx+q$, so the slope is the number multiplying $x$ and nothing else.

$$f(x)=7x+2$$

That coefficient is $7$. The leftover constant $2$ only lifts the graph without changing the tilt: one extra unit of $x$ always raises the height by the same amount.

$$m=7\qquad f(1)-f(0)$$

$$m=9-2$$

$$m=7$$

The slope is $7$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The value at the origin is read by putting $x=0$ into the given line, which kills the slope term and leaves the intercept.

$$f(x)=7x+2$$

$$f(0)=7\cdot 0+2$$

$$f(0)=2$$

That height is also where the graph meets the vertical axis, because that axis is the line $x=0$.

The line meets the vertical axis at height $2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The opening direction is decided by the sign of the square term alone, so read that coefficient from the given formula rather than from a rewritten factorisation.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+6x$$

The number in front of $x^{2}$ is $1$, which is positive, so both arms rise and the turning point is the lowest point of the graph.

$$a=1>0$$

An upward-opening parabola is the opposite of the claimed downward one.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Putting $x=0$ into the given parabola kills every term that still contains $x$, so only a possible constant could survive; here there is none.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+6x$$

$$g(0)=0^{2}+6\cdot 0$$

$$g(0)=0$$

The graph therefore meets the vertical axis at the origin.

The value at zero is $0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The axis of a parabola is the vertical line $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, built from the first two coefficients of the given formula.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+6x\qquad a$$

$$g(x)=1,\ b$$

$$g(x)=6$$

$$x=-3$$

The graph is its own mirror image in that line: the two roots of $g(x)=x(x+6)$ sit at $0$ and $-6$, whose midpoint is $-3$.

The axis is $x=-3$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Both rules are handed over with numbers already in place:

$$
f(x) = 7 x + 2\qquad g(x)
$$

$$
= x \left(x + 6\right)
$$

No work beyond reading is needed for the slope, for the two values at $0$ and for the opening direction, which is upwards here because of the sign in front of $x^{2}$.

$$
m = 7\qquad f(0)
$$

$$
= 2\qquad g(0)
$$

$$
= 0\qquad a
$$

$$
= 1

Since the parabola is concrete, the vertex can be computed once and reused: the axis first, then the height above it.

$$
g(x) = \left(x+3\right)^{2}-9\qquad \text{vertex}

$$
= \left(-3,-9\right)

tasks.title: Reading a Parabola Straight From Its Coefficients
tasks.context: The parabola $p$ is given by $p(x)=2x^{2}-8$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $p$ opens upwards.
The roots of $p$ are $2$ and $-2$.
The graph of $p$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=-8$.
The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=1$.

tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write down the given parabola and read the number in front of $x^{2}$; that single sign decides which way the arms point.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-8$$

The leading coefficient is $2$, which is positive, so both arms of the graph rise and the turning point is the lowest point.

$$a=2>0$$

The graph opens upwards.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The roots are the inputs where the height is zero, so set the given formula equal to zero and divide by the leading coefficient $2$.

$$2x^{2}-8 = 0\iff x^{2}$$

$$= 4$$

$$x=-2\qquad x$$

$$x=2$$

Both values really make $p$ vanish, and a quadratic has no further roots.

The zeros are $-2$ and $2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The vertical intercept is the leftover constant, because every term with $x$ dies at $x=0$.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-8$$

$$p(0)=2\cdot 0^{2}-8$$

$$p(0)=-8$$

That height is the point where the graph meets the $y$-axis.

The graph meets the $y$-axis at $y=-8$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The axis sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, and here there is no $x$ term at all, so $b=0$.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-8\qquad b$$

$$p(x)=0$$

$$x=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 2}$$

$$x=0$$

The mirror line is therefore the vertical coordinate axis. The claim names $x=1$, a different vertical line.

The axis is $x=0$ rather than $x=1$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

With no $x$ term the turning point sits on the vertical axis, so evaluate the given formula there.

$$x=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 2}$$

$$x=0$$

$$p(0)=-8$$

The leading coefficient $2$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and the values never sink below that height; there is no largest value.

The smallest value is $-8$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
There is one graph to study, and it is a parabola.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-8$$

The axis formula fixes the turning point, while the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients with no equation to solve.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(0,-8\right)\qquad S
$$

$$
= 0\qquad P
$$

$$
= -4
$$

Two real roots follow from the positive discriminant, and the axis of symmetry sits exactly halfway between them.

$$
\Delta = 64\qquad x_{1}
$$

$$
= -2\qquad x_{2}

$$
= 2

tasks.title: A Parabola That Turns Downwards
tasks.context: Consider the quadratic function $q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $q$ opens downwards.
The axis of symmetry of $q$ is the line $x=2$.
The largest value taken by $q$ is $8$.
The graph of $q$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=4$.
The equation $q(x)=0$ has two distinct real solutions.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The sign in front of $x^{2}$ decides the opening, so read it off the given formula.

$$q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$$

The leading coefficient is $-3$, which is negative, so both arms fall and the turning point is the highest point of the graph.

$$a=-3<0$$

The graph therefore opens downwards.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Build the axis from the first two coefficients of the given parabola; the constant term never enters this formula.

$$a=-3\qquad b$$

$$a=12$$

$$x=-\frac{12}{2\cdot(-3)}$$

$$x=2$$

The graph is symmetric in that vertical line: a step of size $h$ to the left of $x=2$ produces the same height as the same step to the right.

The axis is $x=2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The extreme value is the height on the axis, so evaluate at the abscissa $x=2$ just obtained from the coefficients.

$$q(2)=-3\cdot 2^{2}+12\cdot 2-4$$

$$q(2)=-12+24-4$$

$$q(2)=8$$

Because $a=-3$ is negative the arms fall on both sides, so $8$ is the largest value and there is no smallest one.

The largest value is $8$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The height on the vertical axis is the constant term of the given formula, already visible without any further work.

$$q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$$

$$q(0)=-4$$

The claim reports $y=4$, which simply drops the minus sign in front of that constant.

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=-4$, not at $y=4$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The number of real zeros is decided by the discriminant $b^{2}-4ac$, so plug in the three coefficients of the given formula.

$$a=-3\qquad b$$

$$a=12\qquad c$$

$$a=-4$$

$$\Delta=12^{2}-4(-3)(-4)$$

$$\Delta=144-48$$

$$\Delta=96$$

A positive discriminant means two distinct real solutions of $q(x)=0$.

There are two distinct real solutions.

So the statement is True.

$$q(x)=-3x^{2}+12x-4$$

tasks.title: Vertex Form Read at a Glance
tasks.context: A parabola is already written in completed-square form: $p(x)=\left(x+3\right)^{2}-7$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The vertex of the graph of $p$ is the point $\left(-3,-7\right)$.
The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=3$.
The graph of $p$ opens upwards.
The smallest value taken by $p$ is $-7$.
Expanding gives $p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The given formula is already in the shape $a(x-h)^{2}+k$, so the turning point can be read without expanding into $ax^{2}+bx+c$.

$$p(x)=(x+3)^{2}-7$$

The square vanishes at $x=-3$, and the leftover constant is the height there.

$$\text{vertex}=(-3,-7)$$

That is the point named in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The axis is the vertical line through the turning point, whose abscissa is the number that cancels the bracket.

$$p(x)=(x+3)^{2}-7$$

$$x+3 = 0\iff x$$

$$p(x)=-3$$

The claim names $x=3$, which is the opposite sign — a common mix-up between $(x+h)^{2}$ and $(x-h)^{2}$.

The axis is $x=-3$ rather than $x=3$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The stretch in front of the square is $1$, already visible in the given completed-square form; no expansion is needed to read it.

$$p(x)=1\cdot(x+3)^{2}-7$$

A positive stretch sends both arms upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph.

$$a=1>0$$

The graph opens upwards.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

In completed-square form the leftover constant is the height of the turning point, and a positive stretch makes that height the smallest value.

$$p(x)=(x+3)^{2}-7$$

The square is never negative, so the values never sink below $-7$, and $-7$ is attained at $x=-3$.

$$p(x)\ge -7$$

The smallest value is $-7$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Expand the given square and collect the powers of $x$; the completed-square form and the expanded form describe the same function.

$$p(x)=(x+3)^{2}-7$$

$$p(x)=(x^{2}+6x+9)-7$$

$$p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$$

Every coefficient agrees with the displayed expansion.

The expanded rule is $x^{2}+6x+2$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:

Multiplying out puts the same rule in standard form, where every coefficient can be read off directly.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+6x+2$$

tasks.title: Zeros Straight From a Product of Factors
tasks.context: A quadratic function is handed over already factored: $q(x)=\left(x-1\right)\left(x+6\right)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The roots of $q$ are $1$ and $-6$.
The two roots of $q$ add up to $-5$.
The graph of $q$ opens downwards.
The graph of $q$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=-6$.
Expanding gives $q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A product vanishes exactly when one of its factors does, so the given brackets already display the roots without any expanding.

$$q(x)=(x-1)(x+6)$$

$$q(x)=0$$

$$x=1\qquad x$$

$$x=-6$$

Each linear equation has one solution, and there are no other zeros.

The roots are $1$ and $-6$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Add the two roots already sitting in the brackets; the sum does not need the quadratic formula.

$$1+(-6)$$

$$=-5$$

The same sum is minus the middle coefficient once the product is expanded, which is a useful check.

$$(x-1)(x+6)=x^{2}+5x-6\qquad S$$

$$(x-1)(x+6)=-\frac{5}{1}$$

$$(x-1)(x+6)=-5$$

The two roots add up to $-5$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The stretch in front of the two brackets is $1$, so the square term that appears on expanding is $x^{2}$ with a positive coefficient.

$$q(x)=(x-1)(x+6)$$

$$q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$$

$$a=1>0$$

A positive leading coefficient sends both arms upwards.

The graph opens upwards, not downwards.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The vertical intercept is the value at $x=0$, which in factored form is just the product of the two constant pieces of the brackets.

$$q(0)=(0-1)(0+6)$$

$$q(0)=-6$$

That height is where the graph meets the $y$-axis, and it matches the constant term of the expansion $x^{2}+5x-6$.

The graph meets the $y$-axis at $y=-6$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Multiply the two brackets out and collect equal powers; the function itself does not change.

$$q(x)=(x-1)(x+6)$$

The middle term is $6x-x=5x$ and the constant is $-1\cdot 6=-6$.

$$q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$$

Every coefficient agrees with the displayed expansion.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Only one parabola is in play here.

$$q(x)=\left(x-1\right)\left(x+6\right)$$

$$q(x)=x^{2}+5x-6$$

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(-\frac{5}{2},-\frac{49}{4}\right)\qquad S
$$

$$
\Delta = 49\qquad x_{1}
$$

$$
= -6\qquad x_{2}
$$

= 1

tasks.title: A Water Tank Draining at a Steady Rate
tasks.context: A tank drains at a steady rate: after $x$ minutes it still holds $V(x)=200-8x$ litres. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Each extra minute changes the volume by $-8$ litres.
At $x=10$ the volume equals $120$ litres.
The volume equals $0$ litres at $x=25$.
Doubling $x$ always doubles the volume.
The volume changes by the same amount for every extra minute.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The model is a line, so one extra minute always changes the volume by the slope. Write the difference $V(x+1)-V(x)$ to see it.

$$V(x)=200-8x$$

$$V(x+1)-V(x)=\bigl(200-8(x+1)\bigr)-\bigl(200-8x\bigr)$$

$$V(x+1)-V(x)=-8$$

The difference does not depend on $x$: every extra minute removes the same $8$ litres.

Each extra minute changes the volume by $-8$ litres.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

After ten minutes the tank still holds whatever the drain model returns at that instant, so substitute $x=10$.

$$V(10)=200-8\cdot 10$$

$$V(10)=200-80$$

$$V(10)=120$$

Ten minutes at $8$ litres per minute remove $80$ litres from the initial $200$, leaving $120$.

The volume at $x=10$ is $120$ litres.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The tank is empty when the linear model hits zero, so isolate $x$ by undoing the subtraction of $8x$.

$$200-8x=0$$

$$x=\frac{200}{8}$$

$$x=25$$

Substituting back confirms the pair:

$$V(25)=200-8\cdot 25$$

$$V(25)=0$$

.

The volume is $0$ litres at $x=25$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Doubling the input doubles the output only when the graph runs through the origin; a constant term is charged once and is not doubled with the rest.

$$V(1)=200-8$$

$$V(1)=192\qquad V(2)$$

$$V(1)=200-16$$

$$V(1)=184$$

Twice the value at $x=1$ would be $384$, whereas the model gives $184$ at $x=2$.

$$V(2)\neq 2\,V(1)$$

The intercept $200$ breaks the proportion between $x$ and the volume.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Equal steps of the input produce equal changes of the volume precisely when the model is a line; a square term would make the steps grow.

$$V(x)=200-8x$$

$$V(x+1)-V(x)=-8$$

The difference is a constant, independent of the minute at which the step is taken.

Every extra minute counts the same $-8$ litres.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem fixes a single line.

$$V(x)=200-8x$$

Ordering the two terms brings the rule into the shape $mx+q$.

$$V(x)=-8x+200$$

Two numbers describe it completely: the slope, which is the change of height per unit step, and the height above the origin.

$$
m = -8\qquad V(0)
$$

$$
= 200
$$

Setting the height to zero locates the single crossing of the $x$-axis, and the sign of the slope fixes the direction once and for all.

$$
-8x+200 = 0\Rightarrow x
$$

$$
= 25
$$

tasks.title: Where a Rising Line Crosses the Axes
tasks.context: The line $u$ is given by $u(x)=4x+10$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $u$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=-\frac{5}{2}$.
The graph of $u$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=10$.
The slope of the graph of $u$ is $10$.
$u$ is increasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A line crosses the horizontal axis where its height is zero, so isolate $x$ by undoing addition and then multiplication.

$$4x+10=0$$

$$x=\frac{-10}{4}$$

$$x=-\frac{5}{2}$$

Substituting the root back gives

$$
u\bigl(-\frac{5}{2}\bigr)=4\cdot\bigl(-\frac{5}{2}\bigr)+10
$$

$$u\bigl(-\frac{5}{2}\bigr)=0$$

, so it is a genuine zero.

The crossing is at $x=-\frac{5}{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The height at $x=0$ is the leftover constant of the given line; the slope contributes nothing on the vertical axis.

$$u(x)=4x+10$$

$$u(0)=4\cdot 0+10$$

$$u(0)=10$$

That height is the intercept $q$ in the shape $mx+q$.

The graph meets the $y$-axis at $y=10$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

In the shape $mx+q$ the slope is the coefficient of $x$, not the constant term. The two numbers play different roles.

$$u(x)=4x+10$$

$$m=4\qquad q$$

$$m=10$$

The number $10$ is the intercept, while one extra unit of $x$ changes the height by $4$.

The slope is $4$, not $10$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

A line rises from left to right precisely when its slope is positive, so compare two neighbouring values.

$$u(x)=4x+10\qquad m$$

$$u(x)=4$$

$$u(0)=10\qquad u(1)$$

$$u(0)=14$$

Each unit step to the right raises the height by $4$, and $4>0$.

A positive slope means $u$ is increasing.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Substitute $x=3$ into the given line $u(x)=4x+10$ and simplify term by term.

$$u(3)=4\cdot 3+10$$

The product is $12$, and adding the intercept $10$ finishes the arithmetic.

$$u(3)=12+10$$

$$u(3)=22$$

The graph therefore passes through the point $(3,22)$.

The value is $22$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem fixes a single line.

$$u(x)=4x+10$$

Two numbers describe it completely: the slope, which is the change of height per unit step, and the height above the origin.

$$
m = 4\qquad u(0)
$$

$$
= 10
$$

Setting the height to zero locates the single crossing of the $x$-axis, and the sign of the slope fixes the direction once and for all.

$$
4x+10 = 0\Rightarrow x
$$

$$
= -\frac{5}{2}
$$

tasks.title: Locating the Peak of a Downward Parabola
tasks.context: The function $h$ is given by $h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $h$ opens downwards.
The axis of symmetry of $h$ is the line $x=3$.
The largest value taken by $h$ is $4$.
The graph of $h$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=5$.
The roots of $h$ are $1$ and $5$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Read the leading coefficient of the given parabola; its sign alone decides the opening.

$$h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$$

The number in front of $x^{2}$ is $-1$, which is negative, so both arms fall and the turning point is the highest point.

$$a=-1<0$$

The graph opens downwards.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Build the axis of $h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$ from the first two coefficients; the constant $-5$ never enters this formula.

$$a=-1\qquad b$$

$$a=6$$

$$x=-\frac{6}{2\cdot(-1)}$$

$$x=3$$

The graph is its own mirror image in that vertical line: a step of size $t$ to the left of $x=3$ produces the same height as the same step to the right.

The axis is $x=3$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The largest value of a downward-opening parabola is the height on the axis $x=3$, so substitute that abscissa into the given formula.

$$h(3)=-3^{2}+6\cdot 3-5$$

$$h(3)=-9+18-5$$

$$h(3)=4$$

With $a=-1<0$ the arms fall on both sides, so there is no smallest value, only this peak.

The largest value is $4$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The vertical intercept is the constant term of the given formula, already visible at a glance.

$$h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$$

$$h(0)=-5$$

The claim reports $y=5$, which drops the minus sign in front of that constant.

The graph cuts the $y$-axis at $y=-5$, not at $y=5$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Set the given formula equal to zero and compute the discriminant first, to see that two distinct real roots exist.

$$\Delta=6^{2}-4(-1)(-5)$$

$$\Delta=36-20$$

$$\Delta=16$$

A positive discriminant gives two distinct roots, delivered by the quadratic formula.

$$x = \frac{-6\pm 4}{-2}\implies x$$

$$\Delta=1\qquad x$$

$$\Delta=5$$

The zeros are $1$ and $5$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything below refers to the same parabola.

$$h(x)=-x^{2}+6x-5$$

Before testing anything, it pays to write down the vertex together with the sum and the product of the roots, all three being coefficient arithmetic.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(3,4\right)\qquad S
$$

$$
= 6\qquad P
$$

$$
= 5
$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis, placed symmetrically around the axis of the parabola.

$$
\Delta = 16\qquad x_{1}
$$

$$
= 1\qquad x_{2}
$$

$$
= 5
$$

The arms open downwards, so the turning point is the highest point of the graph and the largest value is $4$.

tasks.title: A Gentle Slope in Fraction Form
tasks.context: The line $v$ is given by $v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The slope of the graph of $v$ is $\frac{1}{3}$.
The graph of $v$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=6$.
The graph of $v$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=-2$.
Increasing $x$ by $3$ always changes $v$ by $1$.
$v$ is decreasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The given line is already written as $mx+q$, so the slope is the coefficient of $x$.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$$

$$m=\frac{1}{3}$$

One extra unit of $x$ therefore raises the height by $\frac{1}{3}$, the same everywhere along the line.

The slope is $\frac{1}{3}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The graph crosses the horizontal axis where the height is zero, so isolate $x$ by adding $2$ and then multiplying by $3$.

$$\frac{1}{3}x-2=0$$

$$x=6$$

Substituting back gives

$$v(6)=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 6-2$$

$$v(6)=0$$

, so it is a genuine zero.

The crossing is at $x=6$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

At $x=0$ the slope term vanishes, leaving the constant; that constant is the intercept on the vertical axis.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$$

$$v(0)=-2$$

The gentle slope $\frac{1}{3}$ contributes nothing there.

The graph meets the $y$-axis at $y=-2$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

On a line the change of height depends only on the length of the step: it is the slope times that length, never on where the step starts.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$$

$$v(x+3)-v(x)=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 3$$

$$v(x+3)-v(x)=1$$

The starting point of the step never enters the difference, so every increase of $x$ by $3$ raises $v$ by $1$.

Increasing $x$ by $3$ always changes $v$ by $1$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The direction of a line is decided by the sign of its slope. Here that slope is the positive fraction $\frac{1}{3}$.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2\qquad m$$

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}$$

Because the slope is positive, every step to the right raises the height: $v(0)=-2$ while $v(3)=-1$.

The function is increasing, not decreasing.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem fixes a single line.

$$v(x)=\frac{1}{3}x-2$$

Two numbers describe it completely: the slope, which is the change of height per unit step, and the height above the origin.

$$
m = \frac{1}{3}\qquad v(0)
$$

$$
= -2
$$

Setting the height to zero locates the single crossing of the $x$-axis, and the sign of the slope fixes the direction once and for all.

$$
\frac{1}{3}x-2 = 0\Rightarrow x
$$

$$
= 6
$$

tasks.title: Constant Second Differences in a Table
tasks.context: A function was sampled at five consecutive whole numbers and the results were collected in the table below. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first differences of the $y$-values are constant.
The second differences of the $y$-values are constant and equal to $2$.
The table is consistent with a quadratic model.
The table is produced by the rule $y=x^{2}+1$.
Continuing the pattern, the value at $x=5$ is $26$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

List the five outputs from the table and subtract neighbours; constant first differences would be the fingerprint of a line.

$$y:\ 1,\ 2,\ 5,\ 10,\ 17$$

$$\text{first differences}:\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$$

The steps come in four different sizes, so they are not constant.

The first differences move.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Differencing the first differences once more produces the second differences, which for a quadratic rule are constant.

$$\text{first differences}:\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

They are all equal to $2$, the value the claim names.

The second differences are constant and equal to $2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Constant second differences with moving first differences are the fingerprint of a quadratic rule, not of a line.

$$
\text{first}:\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7\qquad\text{second}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2
$$

A line would have needed constant first differences, which these rows do not have. For spacing $1$, the second difference $2$ also equals $2a$, so $a=1$.

The table matches a quadratic model.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Substitute the claimed rule into every row of the table; for a quadratic, matching three rows already pins the rule down, and the remaining two are a check.

$$y=x^{2}+1$$

$$
0\mapsto 1,\quad 1\mapsto 2,\quad 2\mapsto 5,\quad 3\mapsto 10,\quad 4\mapsto 17
$$

Every listed pair is reproduced.

The table is produced by $y=x^{2}+1$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The next first-difference grows by the constant second difference $2$, so add $7+2=9$ to the last height $17$.

$$17+9$$

$$=26$$

The same height comes from the quadratic rule already identified.

$$5^{2}+1$$

$$=26$$

The value at $x=5$ is $26$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem, so read it as a list of pairs.

$$\left(0,1\right),\ \left(1,2\right),\ \left(2,5\right),\ \left(3,10\right),\ \left(4,17\right)$$

The inputs are equally spaced, which makes the differences of neighbouring outputs the fastest diagnostic tool available.

$$\text{first}:\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7\qquad \text{second}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

The first differences move while the second ones stand still, the signature of a parabola; the constant second difference is twice the leading coefficient times the squared spacing.

$$y=x^{2}+1$$

tasks.title: A Stretched Parabola and Its Turning Point
tasks.context: The parabola $p$ is given by $p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=2$.
The vertex of the graph of $p$ is the point $\left(2,-5\right)$.
The smallest value taken by $p$ is $7$.
The leading coefficient of $p$ is $3$.
$p$ is decreasing for every $x<2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Build the axis from the first two coefficients of the given parabola; the constant $7$ never enters this formula.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7\qquad a$$

$$p(x)=3,\ b$$

$$p(x)=-12$$

$$x=-\frac{-12}{2\cdot 3}$$

$$x=2$$

The graph is symmetric in that vertical line.

The axis is $x=2$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The turning point of $p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$ sits on the axis $x=2$, so evaluate the given formula there.

$$p(2)=3\cdot 2^{2}-12\cdot 2+7$$

$$p(2)=12-24+7$$

$$p(2)=-5$$

The vertex is therefore the point $(2,-5)$, and because $a=3>0$ it is the lowest point of the graph.

That is the point named in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The smallest value of an upward-opening parabola is the vertex height, not the constant term sitting at the end of the formula.

$$p(2)=-5$$

The leading coefficient $3$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and the values never sink below $-5$.

$$p(x)\ge -5$$

The smallest value is $-5$, not the intercept $7$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The leading coefficient is the number multiplying $x^{2}$ in the given formula, already visible without expanding anything.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$$

$$a=3$$

Its sign tells the opening and its size tells how narrow the parabola is.

The leading coefficient is $3$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A parabola changes direction exactly once, at its axis $x=2$. With a positive stretch the graph falls on everything to the left of the axis and rises on everything to its right.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7\qquad a$$

$$p(x)=3>0$$

$$x<2\implies p\text{ is decreasing}$$

The half-line $x<2$ lies entirely on the decreasing side of the axis.

$p$ is decreasing for every $x<2$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
A single quadratic rule carries every claim.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-12x+7$$

Two standard readings cover most of what follows: the vertex from the completed square, and the sum and product of the roots from the coefficients.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(2,-5\right)\qquad S
$$

$$
= 4\qquad P
$$

$$
= \frac{7}{3}
$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis.

$$\Delta=60$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-5$.
